'''breaker''' (brā′kėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brekere''; < ''break'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who or that which breaks anything, as a machine to crush ores, stones, and other hard substances. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A coal-getter or -hewer; one who breaks down the coal so that it can be conveyed away to the place where it is raised to the surface. [Somersetshire, Eng.] (''b'') A structure in which coal is broken, sized, and prepared for market. [Anthracite region of Penn.] (''c'') One whose occupation it is to break up old ships; a ship-breaker. (''d'') ''Milit.'', a cup-shaped covering, usually made of lead, which serves to break a tube of glass or plaster of Paris at the proper time for igniting the charge in fuses of a certain construction. ''Farrow'', Mil. Encyc. (''e'') In ''cotton-manuf.'', a breaking-engine (which see). (''f'') In ''linen-manuf.'', a carding-machine to the action of which the tow is first subjected. (''g'') A light, strong plow for breaking new ground.} '''2.''' A violator or transgressor: as, a ''breaker'' of the law.—'''3.''' A wave broken into foam against the shore, a sand-bank, or a rock near the surface: generally in the plural.
{{smaller block|<poem>The night-winds sigh, the ''breakers'' roar,
And shrieks the wild sea-mew.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, i. 13.}}}}
'''4.''' [In this sense perhaps a corruption of Sp. ''barrica'', a keg.] A small water-cask used in boats to supply the crew with water and for ballast.—'''5.''' A trainer, as of horses or dogs. ='''Syn. 3.''' {{smaller|See ''wave''.}}

'''breakfast''' (brek′fast), ''n.'' [Late ME. ''brekefaste''; < ''break'' + ''fast''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' Cf. F. ''déjeuner'', a breakfast, < ''déjeuner'', break fast: see ''déjeuner''.] '''1.''' The first meal in the day; the meal by which one breaks the fast lasting from the previous day; the food eaten at the first meal.—'''2.''' A meal or food in general.

'''breaking-diameter''' (brā′king-dī-am″e-tėr), ''n.'' The diameter of a test specimen of metal at the point of rupture when subjected to tensile stress. {{smaller|It is measured and used to determine the area of the cross-section at that point after rupture. The comparison of this area with the original area of the same cross-section gives the degree of constriction or the percentage, technically called the ''contraction of area.''}}

'''breaking-engine''' (brā′king-en″jin), ''n.'' In ''cotton-manuf.'', the first carding-machine following the lapper; a breaker.

'''breaking-frame''' (brā′king-frām), ''n.'' A machine for splicing and stretching slivers of wool.

'''breaking-weight''' (brā′king-wāt), ''n.'' The weight which must be hung from a rod of given cross-section or placed upon any structure in order to break it. It measures the cohesion of the material experimented upon.
{{smaller block|The floor was loaded with pig-iron to one-fourth of its ''breaking-weight.''
{{right|''Workshop Receipts'', 2d ser., p. 293.}}}}

'''break-iron''' (brāk′ī″ėrn), ''n.'' In carpenters’ planes with double irons, the top or front iron, the lower edge of which is in contact with the face of the lower cutting-iron just above its cutting edge. As the shaving is cut, the break-iron turns or breaks it away from the wood.

'''break-lathe''' (brāk′lāᴛ̵ʜ), ''n.'' A lathe having a gap in its bed, in order to increase its swing or capacity for turning objects of large radius; a gap-lathe or gap-bed lathe. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''breakman''', ''n.'' See ''brakeman.''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|break|670|breakman}}</noinclude>{{smaller|(''b'') To be dissipated or disappear, as fog or clouds.—'''To break down.''' (''a'') To come down by breaking: as, the coach ''broke down.'' (''b'') To fail in any undertaking through incapacity, miscalculation, emotion, embarrassment, or loss of health.}}
{{smaller block|Some dozen women did double duty, and then were blamed for ''breaking down.''
{{right|''L. M. Alcott'', Hospital Sketches, p. 68.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') To lose one’s health; become sick. (''d'') To be overcome by emotion; weep. (''e'') To granulate, as gunpowder.—'''To break forth.''' (''a'') To burst out; be suddenly manifested; exhibit sudden activity: as, a cry ''broke forth.''}}
{{smaller block|<poem>His malice ’gainst the lady
Will suddenly ''break forth.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Break forth'', ye hearts that frozen winters bind
In icy chains more strong than close the year!</poem>
{{right|''Jones Very'', Poems, p. 46.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To rush or issue out. (''c'') To give vent to one’s feelings; burst out: as, to ''break forth'' with fury; to “''break forth'' into singing,” Isa. xliv. 23.—'''To break from,''' to disengage one’s self from; leave abruptly or violently.—'''To break in,''' to leave the point, and start to chase game: said of a dog on point.—'''To break into.''' (''a'') To enter by force, especially burglariously: as, to ''break into'' a house. In ''law'', opening a latched door, or pushing open an unfastened but closed sash, may be a breaking which will constitute burglary. (''b'') To break forth into.}}
{{smaller block|It is very natural for men who are abridged in one excess to ''break into'' some other.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, lviii.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To break in upon,''' to intrude upon suddenly or violently.—'''To break loose,''' to get free by force; escape from confinement by violence; shake off restraint.—'''To break off.''' (''a'') To part; become separated: as, the branch ''broke off.'' (''b'') To desist suddenly.}}
{{smaller block|Do not ''break off'' so. {{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To break off from,''' to part from with violence.—'''To break out.''' (''a'') To issue forth; arise or spring up: as, a fire ''breaks out''; a sedition ''breaks out''; a fever ''breaks out.'' (''b'') To appear in eruptions: said of certain diseases; to have pustules or an efflorescence on the skin: said of a person. (''c'') To throw off restraint and become dissolute: as, after living quietly he again ''broke out.'' (''d'') To give vent to the feelings impetuously by speech.}}
{{smaller block|As soon as my uncle Toby was seated by the fire, and had filled his pipe, my father ''broke out'' in this manner.
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, ix. 32.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To break sheer''' (''naut.''), to be forced the wrong way by the wind or current, so as not to lie well for keeping clear of the anchor: said of a ship at anchor.—'''To break shot,''' to leave the point, when the gun is discharged, to chase game: said of a dog on point.—'''To break through.''' (''a'') To disregard or overcome: as, to ''break through'' all restraint or reserve. (''b'') To act contrary to; violate with impunity: as, to ''break through'' a law (in such a manner as to avoid the penalty).—'''To break up.''' (''a'') To dissolve and separate: as, a company ''breaks up;'' a meeting ''breaks up;'' the ice ''breaks up;'' a fog ''breaks up.''}}
{{smaller block|We went into Mrs. Mercer’s, and there mighty merry, smutting one another with candle grease and soot, till most of us were like devils. And that being done, then we ''broke up'', and to my house.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, II. 430.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') In ''alg.'', said of an equation or quantic when in consequence of particular relations between its coefficients it reduces to a product of factors of lower degree.—'''To break with.''' (''a'') To part in enmity from; cease to be friends with; quarrel with: as, to ''break with'' a friend or companion.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Be not afraid to ''break''
''With'' murderers and traitors.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline.}}}}
{{smaller block|He had too much consideration and authority in the country for her to wish to ''break with'' him.
{{right|''Prescott.''}}}}
{{smaller|(''b''†) To broach a subject to; make a disclosure to.}}
{{smaller block|But perceiving this great alteration in his friend, he thought fit to ''break with'' him thereof.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If thou dost love fair Hero, cherish it;
And I will ''break with'' her, and ''with'' her father,
And thou shalt have her.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, i. 1.}}}}

'''break''' (brāk), ''n.''   [In most senses of mod. origin from the verb ''break'', the older noun being ''breach'' with its variants: see ''breach''. In some senses merely a different spelling of the related ''brake''<sup>3</sup>, q. v.]   '''1.''' A forcible disruption or separation of parts; a gap or opening made by breaking; a fracture, rupture, or breach: as, a ''break'' in a wall, a beam, or a garment.—'''2.''' A breaking off; an interruption of continuity; a sudden stoppage or suspension; a gap between parts; specifically, in ''printing'', the gap between two paragraphs.
{{smaller block|<poem>All modern trash is
Set forth with numerous ''breaks'' and dashes. {{right|''Swift.''}}</poem>

{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 125.}}}}
'''3.''' A breaking or bursting out or away; a sudden or marked transition from one course, place, or state to another: as, a ''break'' of the voice; the ''break'' of day; the prisoner made a ''break'' for freedom.
{{smaller block|The several emotions of mind, and ''breaks'' of passion, in this speech, are admirable. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 106.}}}}
'''4.''' In ''arch.'': (''a'') A distinct variation in the style of a part of a building from that of other parts; the place where such a change occurs in the design, or the junction in the building of two distinct styles or designs. (''b'') A recess or projection from the general surface of any architectural part or feature.—'''5.''' In ''hat-making'', the angle formed by the body and the brim of a hat.—'''6.''' In a ship, the part where a deck terminates and the descent to the next deck begins.—'''7.''' A contrivance to check the velocity of a wheeled carriage; a brake. See ''brake''<sup>3</sup>, 9.—'''8.''' In ''teleg.'': (''a'') A commutator or contrivance for interrupting or changing the direction of electric currents. (''b'') An interruption of the continuity of a conductor.—'''9.''' In ''music'': (''a'') The point in the scale where the quality of voice of one register changes to that of another, as from tenor to alto or from alto to soprano. (''b'') The point where the chest-voice changes to the head-voice. (''c'') The point where a similar change occurs in a musical wind-instrument: {{img float|file=century v01 p0696 c2f1.png|width=137px|align=left|cap=}} thus, in the clarinet such a change occurs between the notes B flat and B natural. (''d'') The singing, or the sounding on a trumpet or horn, from lack of ability, care, or skill, of a note different from the one intended to be produced. (''e'') A note which a singer produces more imperfectly or with greater difficulty than the notes above or below it. (''f'') In an organ-stop, the sudden change in the proper scale-series of pipes to a series lower in pitch. (''g'') In ''organ-building'', the points in the scale of stops having more than one pipe to a note, where for any reason the relative pitch of the pipes is altered: especially applied to mixture-stops having several pipes to each note.—'''10.''' In a bakery, a bench on which, or a machine by which, dough is kneaded.—'''11.''' In ''mining'', a crack or fissure caused by the sinking of strata. —'''12.''' In ''type-founding'', a piece of metal next the shank of a type which is broken off in finishing. —'''13.''' On the stock exchange, a sudden decline in prices.—'''14.''' In ''pool'', the shot that breaks or scatters the balls as piled together at the beginning of the game; hence, the first shot or play, or the right to the first play: as, it is my ''break''.—'''15.''' In ''fort.'', same as ''brisure'', 1.—'''16.''' A large, high-set, four-wheeled vehicle, with a straight body and a seat in front for the driver and another behind for footmen.—'''17.''' A regular sale of tobacco at the time when the hogsheads are first opened. [Local, Virginia.]—'''18.''' The quantity of hemp prepared in one year.
{{smaller block|Best St. Petersburg clean Hemp of the ''break'' of the year 1796.
{{right|''Mass. Mercury'', April 29, 1796.}}}}
'''19.''' Same as ''breck'', 4.—'''Break of day''', {{smaller|the first appearance of light in the morning; the dawn; daybreak.}}
{{smaller block|He arrived with his guide, a little after ''break of day'', at Charing-cross.
{{right|''Addison'', Foxhunter at a Masquerade.}}}}

'''Act’s breakfast.''' {{smaller|See ''act.''}}

'''breakfast''' (brek′fa̤st), ''v.''   [< ''breakfast, n.''; orig. two words, ''break fast.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To furnish with the first meal in the day; supply with breakfast.

{{smaller block|First, sir, I read, and then I ''breakfast.''

'''breakfast-cap''' (brek′fa̤st-kap), ''n.'' A small cap, usually made of muslin or lace and ribbons, worn at breakfast by married women.

{{right|''C. D. Warner,'' Backlog Studies, p. 71.}}}}

{{smaller block|No ''breakfastings'' with them, which consume a great deal of time. {{right|''Chesterfield.''}}}}
